paragraphs.heading: Four shared electrons
paragraphs.text: A double bond is a covalent bond in which two atoms share four bonding electrons, where a single bond uses two. Most often it joins two carbon atoms, as in the alkenes. It can also join different elements, such as carbon and oxygen in a carbonyl group. Other familiar examples are N=N in azo compounds, C=N in imines and S=O in sulfoxides.

paragraphs.heading: How it is drawn
paragraphs.text: In a skeletal formula, a double bond appears as two parallel lines between the joined atoms, which in print is simply the equals sign. The Russian chemist Alexander Butlerov brought double bonds into chemical notation.

paragraphs.heading: Sigma plus pi
paragraphs.text: Orbital hybridisation explains how this bond works. In ethylene, each carbon has three sp² orbitals lying flat in one plane at roughly 120° to each other, plus one p-orbital standing at right angles to that plane. As the two carbons approach, two sp² orbitals overlap to make a sigma bond. At the same time the two p-orbitals come together and form a pi bond.

paragraphs.heading: Shorter, stronger, locked
paragraphs.text: For the p-orbitals to overlap as much as possible they must stay parallel, so the atoms cannot rotate around a double bond. This locked shape is what gives rise to cis-trans isomerism. Double bonds involving carbon are shorter and stronger than single bonds: the C=C bond in ethylene is 133 pm long, against 154 pm for the C−C bond in ethane. It is stronger too, 636 versus 368 kJ mol⁻¹, but not twice as strong, because the pi bond overlaps less effectively and is weaker than the sigma bond.

paragraphs.heading: Chains and rings
paragraphs.text: When double and single bonds alternate, p-orbital overlap can stretch along several atoms in a chain, making a conjugated system. Conjugation turns up in dienes and enones, and in ring-shaped molecules it can lead to aromaticity. In cumulenes, by contrast, two double bonds sit right next to each other without overlapping.

paragraphs.heading: Heavier elements
paragraphs.text: Double bonds are common for carbon, nitrogen and oxygen, the period 2 elements, and less common for elements in later periods, a pattern called the double bond rule. Even so, alkene-like compounds R₂E=ER₂ are now known for every heavier group 14 element. Unlike alkenes, these are not flat but twisted or trans bent, and the effect grows stronger for the heavier elements. Some double bonds in plumbenes and stannenes are about as strong as hydrogen bonds.
